clinicalPearls: An uncommon cold-antibody haemolytic anaemia causing acute intravascular haemolysis after cold exposure
It is most often seen in children following a viral infection and is usually self-limiting
The causative Donath-Landsteiner antibody is a biphasic IgG that binds red cells in the cold and fixes complement on rewarming
The antibody classically has specificity for the P antigen
Presentation is with fever, back or abdominal pain, pallor and passage of dark (haemoglobinuric) urine
Management is supportive with keeping warm and transfusion if needed; most childhood cases resolve spontaneously
reference.pathophysiology: Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria is mediated by the Donath-Landsteiner antibody, a biphasic IgG autoantibody usually directed at the P antigen. In the cooler peripheral circulation the antibody binds red cells and fixes early complement components; when the cells return to the warmer central circulation, the complement cascade completes, causing intravascular haemolysis and haemoglobinuria. It frequently follows a viral illness, particularly in children, and the transient antibody explains the self-limiting course.
additionalInvestigations: Direct antiglobulin test (often positive for complement only)
Full blood count, reticulocytes and haemolysis markers
redFlags: Severe acute anaemia with haemodynamic compromise
Massive intravascular haemolysis with renal impairment
Recurrent episodes suggesting an underlying disorder
Very dark urine with rapidly falling haemoglobin
reference.prognosis: The post-viral childhood form is usually acute and self-limiting with an excellent prognosis; chronic or recurrent disease is rarer and may relate to an underlying condition.
pitfalls: Confusing it with cold agglutinin disease (different antibody and mechanism)
Failing to keep the patient warm during care and transfusion
Overlooking haemoglobinuria as a sign of intravascular haemolysis
